questions.stem: Cost price ₹400, selling price ₹460. The profit percent is:
questions.explanation: TYPE 1 — basic profit%. Profit = 460 − 400 = 60. Profit% = 60/400 × 100 = 15%. Base is always CP. Watch: if the question had asked 'profit on SP' the base would flip; examiners test this confusion.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: An article is sold at ₹1080 for a profit of 20%. The cost price was:
questions.explanation: TYPE 3 — find CP from SP + profit%. SP is 120% of CP → CP = 1080 × 100/120 = 900. Distractor ₹864 is 1080 × 0.8 (wrongly subtracting 20%); ₹960 is 1080 × 100/112.5.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: A man sells two watches at ₹2400 each. He gains 20% on one and loses 20% on the other. The net result is:
questions.explanation: TYPE 4 — same SP, opposite %. Always a net LOSS of x²/100 %. Here 20²/100 = 4%. Verify: CP1 = 2400×100/120 = 2000; CP2 = 2400×100/80 = 3000. Total CP 5000, SP 4800 → loss 200 on 5000 = 4%.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: An article is marked 25% above cost price and sold at 10% discount. The profit percent is:
questions.explanation: TYPE 5 — mark-up + discount → profit. Successive % rule: +25 and −10 give 25 − 10 − (25×10)/100 = 15 − 2.5 = +12.5%. Verify: CP 100 → MP 125 → SP 125 × 0.9 = 112.5 → profit 12.5%.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks goods 40% above cost price and wants a net profit of 12%. The discount he must offer is:
questions.explanation: TYPE 6 — back-solve discount. SP/CP = 1.12, MP/CP = 1.40, so SP/MP = 1.12/1.40 = 0.80. Discount = 20%. Verify: CP 100 → MP 140 → SP 112 → discount on MP = 28/140 = 20%.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: A dealer uses a 900 g weight for 1 kg while selling at cost price. His profit percent is approximately:
questions.explanation: TYPE 7 — false weight. He charges for 1000 g but gives 900 g. Extra = 100 g on actual 900 g delivered. Profit% = 100/900 × 100 = 11.11%. Distractor 10% uses the wrong base (charged qty); 9.09% inverts the ratio.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: By selling at ₹810, a man loses 10%. The price at which he should sell to gain 10% is:
questions.explanation: TYPE 9 — chain via CP. 810 = 90% of CP → CP = 900. For 10% gain: SP = 110% × 900 = 990. Distractor ₹970 mis-adds ₹20 profit to 810; ₹1010 uses 112%.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: Two successive discounts of 10% and 20% are equivalent to a single discount of:
questions.explanation: TYPE 11 — equivalent single discount. Formula: 10 + 20 − (10 × 20)/100 = 30 − 2 = 28%. The naïve 30% (just adding) is the classic trap; 26% subtracts the cross term instead of adding it back.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: A shopkeeper's profit is 20% of the selling price. His profit percent on cost price is:
questions.explanation: TYPE 12 — profit stated on SP. Let SP = 100; profit = 20; so CP = 80. Profit% on CP = 20/80 × 100 = 25%. The 20% distractor is the naïve reading that ignores which base the stated 20% sits on.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude

questions.stem: An article's cost increases by 20% but the selling price remains the same. If the original profit was 40%, the new profit percent is:
questions.explanation: VARIATION on TYPE 3 — CP changes, SP fixed. Take CP = 100 → SP = 140. New CP = 120, SP unchanged 140. New profit% = 20/120 × 100 = 16.67%. Distractor 14.28% uses 20/140 (wrong base); 10% thinks the margin collapses by 30.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
